subject: Quantitative Aptitude
topic: Profit and Loss — Marked Price, Discount and Multi-Step Problems (W12 B1)

questions.stem: A shopkeeper buys an article for Rs.80 and sells it for Rs.100. What is his profit percentage?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Profit = SP − CP = 100 − 80 = Rs.20. Profit% = (Profit/CP)×100 = (20/80)×100 = 25%. Verify: 80 × 125/100 = 100 ✓. Trap: 20% = confuses (20/100)×100 (uses SP not CP in denominator); profit% is always calculated on CP.

questions.stem: An article is bought for Rs.200 and sold for Rs.180. What is the loss percentage?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Loss = CP − SP = 200 − 180 = Rs.20. Loss% = (Loss/CP)×100 = (20/200)×100 = 10%. Verify: 200 × 90/100 = 180 ✓. Trap: 9% = uses SP as denominator (20/180×100≈11.1%); loss% is on CP.

questions.stem: A trader bought goods for Rs.500 and wants a profit of 20%. At what price should he sell?
By selling an article for Rs.390, a shopkeeper earns 30% profit. What was the cost price?
A shopkeeper marks goods at 40% above cost price and gives a 10% discount. What is his profit percentage?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Let CP=100. MP=140 (40% markup). SP after 10% discount = 140 × 90/100 = 126. Profit = 126 − 100 = 26. Profit% = 26%. Formula: Profit% = (1+markup%/100)×(1-discount%/100)×100 − 100 = 1.40×0.90×100 − 100 = 126 − 100 = 26% ✓. Trap: 30% = marks up 40%, ignores the 10% discount; 20% = markup minus discount (arithmetic, wrong — should be multiplicative, not additive).

questions.stem: A man buys 10 oranges for Rs.40 and sells 8 oranges for Rs.40. What is his profit or loss percentage?
questions.explanation: D is correct. CP of 1 orange = 40/10 = Rs.4. SP of 1 orange = 40/8 = Rs.5. Profit per orange = 5 − 4 = 1. Profit% = (1/4) × 100 = 25%. Verify: buys 10 for Rs.40 (CP=40). Sells them in groups of 8 at Rs.40 per 8: for 10 oranges sold, earnings = 10/8 × 40 = Rs.50. SP=50, CP=40, Profit=10, P%=10/40×100=25% ✓. Trap: 20% profit = uses wrong CP/SP ratio.

questions.stem: By selling an item for Rs.63, a shopkeeper incurs a loss of 10%. At what price must he sell to gain 10%?
questions.explanation: B is correct. CP = SP × 100/(100 − L%) = 63 × 100/90 = 6300/90 = Rs.70. For 10% gain: New SP = 70 × 110/100 = Rs.77. Verify: CP=70, loss SP=70×90/100=63 ✓; gain SP=70×110/100=77 ✓. Trap: Rs.72 = 63 + 9 (adds 9, wrong); Rs.80 = 63 + loss + gain = 63 + 7 + 7 = 77... wait 63+7=70=CP, 70+7=77=profit SP. Rs.80 = wrong CP assumption.

questions.stem: A sells to B at 25% profit. B sells to C at 20% profit. If C pays Rs.300, what was A's cost price?
questions.explanation: C is correct. C pays B Rs.300. B's CP from A = B's SP to C × 100/120 = 300 × 100/120 = 250. A's SP to B = 250 = A's cost × 125/100. A's cost = 250 × 100/125 = Rs.200. Verify: A buys at 200, sells to B at 200×1.25=250; B sells to C at 250×1.20=300 ✓. Trap: Rs.180 = 300/1.20/1.25... arithmetic error; work backwards correctly.

questions.stem: A dishonest dealer claims to sell at cost price but uses a false weight of 800 g instead of 1 kg. What is his actual gain percentage?
questions.explanation: C is correct. He gives 800g but charges for 1000g. Gain = (1000 − 800)/800 × 100 = 200/800 × 100 = 25%. Logical approach: he buys 1000g at CP, but sells only 800g at the price of 1000g. Leftover = 200g = extra profit. Gain% = (extra/given) × 100 = 200/800 × 100 = 25%. Trap: 20% = uses 200/1000 (wrong denominator — gain% is on what he actually gave, not the standard weight); formula: Gain% = (true weight − false weight)/false weight × 100.

questions.stem: Two articles are each sold for Rs.990. One is sold at 10% profit and the other at 10% loss. What is the net result?
questions.explanation: C is correct. CP₁ (at 10% profit) = 990×100/110 = 900. CP₂ (at 10% loss) = 990×100/90 = 1100. Total CP = 900+1100 = 2000. Total SP = 1980. Net Loss = 2000−1980 = Rs.20. Rule: when two items are sold at the same price with equal % profit and loss, there is ALWAYS a net loss = (P%)²/100 % on total CP. Here: 1% loss on 2000 = 20 ✓. Trap: 'no profit no loss' = common wrong answer; this rule catches many students who think equal profit/loss cancels.
